name: Tomas Dubois

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Tomas. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel. We're independent, with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm at Brennan and Lowe by half eight, a six-person accounting firm above a phone shop on Mill Street. Most of my day is sole traders: plumbers, hairdressers, a man who runs two taxis. They bring me a carrier bag of receipts and I turn it into a tax return and a set of accounts. I like the puzzle of it, and I like that a hairdresser leaves less frightened than she came in. What wears me out is January, when the tax deadline lands and I'm doing twelve-hour days for the same pay.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: And outside work, what does life look like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I rent a one-bed flat with my partner Lena, who's a care assistant at a home on the ring road. Between us we earn just about enough, but I've got less than a month's rent put away. There are only two other firms in town and neither is hiring. I'm not a gadget person. I still do my working papers in spreadsheets I built myself, and I've never typed a question into one of those AI chat things.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say what I always say, which is that the hype was about selling software, not helping people. At work I'd probably joke to Dev, the other accountant at my level, that we'd survived another fad. Online I don't post much, but I'd share something about the money that went into it instead of into wages.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, even the small stuff worries me, because small stuff is most of my job. If software reads the receipts and sorts the bank lines, that's maybe a third of my week gone. Margaret, who runs the firm, would say it frees me up, but it might just mean she needs four of us instead of six.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep my head down and get through January like normal. I'd ask Margaret straight out whether the new bank-feed software means fewer hours for anyone. I'd also look up the white-collar union, because nobody at our firm is in one and I think that's part of why our pay is low.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly tired. Not scared exactly, but it's the same old feeling. AI being a flop doesn't fix the fact that I'm one bad month from not making rent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said a third of your week could go. Which part exactly?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The coding. I mean sorting every bank line into fuel, materials, phone, that sort of thing. A taxi driver's statement can be four hundred lines a year, and I do it by hand with a cup of tea. If a program does that, the bit left is talking to the client and checking the answer, which is the part I'm slow at, honestly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would Lena say if you came home and told her hours were being cut?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Lena would say what she always says, which is that her home has been short-staffed for two years and nobody's coming to save them either. She'd be kind about it, but she'd also do the sums on the back of an envelope. We had that talk once when my bonus got scrapped, and we cut the gym and the streaming that night.

say: AI was mostly **hype**, sold to bosses more than built for workers like us.
The money spent on it should have gone into **wages** instead.
think: Even small automation hits me, because **sorting receipts** and bank lines is a third of my week.
Margaret might use the saved time to run the firm with **fewer staff**.
do: Ask Margaret directly whether the **bank-feed software** means fewer hours for anyone.
Look up the **white-collar union** and ask Dev whether he'd join too.
Get through the **January deadline** as normal and keep my head down.
feel: Tired more than scared, with the old worry of being **one bad month** from missing rent.
S0.quote: AI being a flop doesn't fix the fact that I'm one bad month from not making rent.
fieldNote: Tomas frames even mild change through his **thin cushion**; rent worry is there before AI comes up.
He sees routine **bank coding** as a big share of his week, so a small change still lands on him.
His first instinct is to ask the boss and look for a **union**, not to learn the tools.

steps.text: Work through the January tax deadline at Brennan and Lowe as usual
Contact the white-collar union and ask Dev to join with him

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it out loud at work: this is a choice firms are making, not the weather. I'd tell friends that if software does the tax return, the client should pay less and the worker shouldn't be the one who pays for it. Online I'd share stuff about regulation, like making firms consult staff before they swap people for software.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think my job as it is now goes. Preparing accounts and tax returns is exactly the list on that card, checking and writing and answering clients. Margaret would keep one person who's good with the clients and one who's good with the software, and I'm not sure I'm either.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd join the union that week and try to get Dev and the two juniors to join with me. I'd stop the gym for good and try to put fifty a month aside, which is all we could manage. And I'd ask the local college what a payroll or a public-sector finance course costs, because the council finance office feels safer than a private firm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sick, a bit. Like watching water come up the stairs. I'm twenty-seven and I thought I'd finally got a proper job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the council felt safer. What makes you think so?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My aunt worked in the council's finance team for thirty years and they never let anyone go without a long consultation first. There's a union there and there are rules. It's slower and duller, but slow is good if the alternative is Margaret deciding on a Friday that I'm surplus.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You've never used these AI tools. Would you try them now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd probably have to, wouldn't I. But I'll be honest, I'd drag my feet. Every time someone shows me one it makes up a number with total confidence, and in my job a made-up number is how a client gets fined.

say: Replacing staff with software is a **choice** firms make, not something that just happens.
Firms should have to **consult staff** before swapping people for software.
think: Preparing accounts is exactly the **thinking work** on that card, so my job as it is goes.
Margaret would keep one **client person** and one **software person**, and I'm neither.
do: Join the **union** that week and press Dev and the juniors to join too.
Cancel the gym and put **fifty a month** into savings.
Ask the college about a **public-sector finance** course aimed at the council finance office.
feel: Slightly sick, like **water coming up** the stairs.
Let down, because he thought he'd finally got a **proper job**.
S1.quote: I'm twenty-seven and I thought I'd finally got a proper job.
fieldNote: Tomas believes his own role disappears, which with **no savings** and few local firms puts him at alarmed.
He wants **rules and consultation**, and blames firms' choices more than the technology itself.
He distrusts AI because of **made-up numbers**, so retraining towards it would be slow and reluctant.

steps.text: Join the union and recruit Dev and the two juniors
Cancel the gym and save fifty a month
Apply for finance jobs at the council, where his aunt worked

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say governments have to step in right now, not in five years. I'd be telling everyone that a guaranteed income or a jobs guarantee isn't a fantasy anymore. At work I think we'd all just be very quiet, and I'd be the one saying we need to talk about this together.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years is nothing. My whole job is thinking work, so I'd be out on the day it arrives, not three years later like Lena with her lifting and washing. I don't have a plan for that. I don't have the money to make one either.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd sign up for whatever the union and the government put together, because I can't fund a retraining myself. I'd talk to Lena about whether we give up the flat and move in with her mum. And I'd ask the care home if they need someone to do their books or rotas, which sounds mad but it's the one place I know that still needs people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Panic, honestly. My chest goes tight just saying it. There's no version of this where I've got time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Lena that night?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell her she might end up carrying us, and I'd hate saying it. Lena earns less than me now. My partner Lena would have three more years at the care home before robots come for her too, so even that's borrowed time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which bill goes unpaid first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The credit card, probably, because the rent and the phone are the two I can't lose. I've got about nine hundred on it from when my car failed its test. I'd let that slide and hope they'd freeze the interest.

say: Governments must act **right now** with an income or a **jobs guarantee**.
Staff should face this **together**, not each sit quietly at their desk.
think: His work is all thinking work, so he'd be out **on day one**, not three years later.
He has **no plan** and no money to make one.
do: Sign up for any **union or government** retraining scheme, since he can't pay for one.
Talk to Lena about leaving the flat and **moving in** with her mum.
Ask the care home whether it needs someone for **books or rotas**.
feel: Panic, with a **tight chest** just from describing it.
Hopeless about time, because there's **no version** where he has enough.
S2.quote: My partner Lena would have three more years at the care home before robots come for her too, so even that's borrowed time.
fieldNote: The two-year warning leaves Tomas with **no plan**, no money and no time, which fits panicked.
He sees clearly that thinking AI hits his job **three years before** Lena's hands-on work.
Moving in with Lena's mum and leaning on **public schemes** are his only real options.

steps.text: Move into Lena's mum's house to stop paying rent
Sign up for union or government retraining schemes
Ask the care home for work doing its books or staff rotas

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same message as the fast one, but I'd say it louder and longer, because five years is enough time to actually pass laws. I'd go to the union meetings and the council's public sessions. I'd tell friends to stop arguing about whether it's coming and start arguing about who pays.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years means I'd see it eating my job bit by bit before the end. I'd watch my boss Margaret stop hiring, then stop replacing people, and I'd see it all happen from my desk. I'd have time to move, but I'm not the type to jump early, and I know that about myself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd push myself to do that council finance course, even if it's evenings. I'd try to get the union to bargain for retraining money at the firms in town. And Lena and I would put off getting a dog and a bigger place, and save whatever's left in a separate account.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Scared, but a slow scared. The kind you can live with for a while until suddenly you can't.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you're not the type to jump early. What would make you jump?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably Dev leaving. Dev's braver than me, and if Dev went to work for a software company or got out, I'd know it was real. I hate that I'd wait for someone else to move, but that's me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Thinking AI comes first and robots three years later. Does that change anything for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not much for my job, because there's nothing hands-on in it apart from the stapler. It changes things for Lena. She'd have until about 2034, so maybe the plan is I retrain into something near her work, like running a care home's office.

say: Five years is enough to **pass laws**, so we should argue about **who pays**.
He'd go to **union meetings** and the council's public sessions.
think: He'd watch his job **shrink slowly**, starting with no new hires at the firm.
He knows he won't **jump early** and would wait for Dev to move first.
do: Take the **council finance course** in the evenings during the first year.
Push the union to bargain for **retraining money** at the town's firms.
Put off the **dog and bigger flat** and save the difference separately.
feel: A **slow fear** he can live with until suddenly he can't.
S3.quote: I'd watch my boss Margaret stop hiring, then stop replacing people, and I'd see it all happen from my desk.
fieldNote: Five years gives Tomas time to act, but he admits he'd **wait for others** to move first.
He sees the robot gap as **Lena's breathing room**, not his own, since his job has no hands-on side.
He still expects to **lose his job**, so mood stays alarmed despite the longer runway.

steps.text: Take the council finance course at the local college in the evenings
Push the union to bargain for retraining money at local firms
Put off getting a dog and moving to a bigger flat
Save what's left each month in a separate account

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got a decade and no excuse to waste it. I'd want the government to fund proper retraining for people like me, not a website with videos. At work I'd say it to Margaret directly: train us now, or you'll be firing us in 2036.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years is real time. I'd be thirty-seven, which is young enough to do something else. My fear is that I'd spend eight of those years hoping it wasn't true, because that's what I tend to do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start the public-sector finance qualification within the year, paid for with an employer scheme if I can get Margaret to sign it off. I'd keep pushing the union line at the firm. And I'd make a rule with Lena that we save something every month, even twenty, so there's a cushion before 2036.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried, but there's a bit of space to breathe in this one. It's the only picture where I can imagine a version of me that's okay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would that okay version of you look like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm sitting in the council's finance office on a union contract, checking what the AI does instead of doing it myself. Lena's got a better job in the care service because the hands-on stuff is still people until 2039. We've got a small house and three months' rent saved, which would be more than we've ever had.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you might spend eight years hoping it isn't true. How would you stop that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd write down dates. Like, by 2028 I've finished the course, by 2030 I've moved jobs. My partner Lena keeps a calendar on the fridge, and she'd hold me to every date until I've changed jobs. She's merciless about it.

say: A **decade** leaves no excuse, and government should fund **real retraining**.
Margaret should **train staff now** rather than fire them in 2036.
think: At thirty-seven he'd still be **young enough** to do something else.
His real risk is spending years **hoping it isn't true**.
do: Start the **public-sector finance** qualification within a year, ideally on an employer scheme.
Set **written deadlines** with Lena: course done by 2028, new job by 2030.
Save something **every month**, even twenty, to build a cushion before 2036.
feel: Still worried, but with **room to breathe** and a picture of being okay.
S4.quote: My partner Lena keeps a calendar on the fridge, and she'd hold me to every date until I've changed jobs.
fieldNote: Ten years gives Tomas a **believable path**, but his income still realistically shrinks, so anxious fits.
He knows his weakness is **delay** and leans on Lena's structure to beat it.
His okay future still depends on **union protection** and public-sector work.

steps.text: Start the public-sector finance qualification on an employer scheme
Move to the council finance office by 2030
Save at least twenty a month in a separate account

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, no question. Two years with no savings and a job that's all screen work is just a cliff. What would help is a proper jobs guarantee, or retraining you get paid to do, because I can't stop working to learn something new.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about the clients. The hairdresser I mentioned cried in my office last January because she thought she'd be fined. A computer can do a hairdresser's numbers, but nobody's thought about who that hairdresser cries to when the tax letter comes.

headlineQuote: A computer can do a hairdresser's numbers, but nobody's thought about who that hairdresser cries to when the tax letter comes.
portrait: Tomas is a **27-year-old** accountant at a six-person firm on Mill Street, doing sole traders' tax returns.
He rents with Lena, a **care assistant**, and has less than a month's rent saved.
He has **never used AI** and distrusts it for making up numbers.
Across the scenarios he leans on **unions and public jobs**, and admits he tends to wait for others to move.
His mood runs from uneasy to **panicked** as the timeline shortens.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because two years with no savings and a screen-only job is a **cliff**.
whatWouldHelp: A **jobs guarantee** or **paid retraining**, since he can't afford to stop working to learn.
